toc.title: Fear is mobilization that can't move
What this has to do with your trauma work
1. Develop the strength of your safety state

blocks.p: Fear is probably a major obstacle in your trauma recovery. Let's look at what fear is, through a story about a police officer, and then three ways to reduce it.

A while back, Mercedes, the former co-host of Stuck Not Broken, and I did a presentation for a group of police officers in a school district. It's one of those districts big enough to have its own police force. Not security guards, not campus monitors: actual police officers assigned to the school district, who also work as regular on-call officers at night.

We were doing these presentations on the Polyvagal Theory for teachers, staff, therapists, nurses, and the police as well. We were teaching about the defensive states: how, when we get stuck there or experience them in the moment, they can be felt as anxiety, or depression, or anger.

One of the officers balked at the idea of being in a defensive state. "No, you're either made for this job or you're not. That has no place in what we do." The others echoed that. It seemed to be common knowledge among them: either you're made for this or you're not.
Mercedes and I like a challenge, so we pushed back a little. "You've never experienced panic on the job? You've never been scared, seriously? You never worry about your safety?"

One of them said no. He was a big guy, probably a higher-up, maybe a sergeant. You could tell he'd been there a while. He said, "I can honestly say that I don't get scared. When I'm activated for a call, I'm focused and I'm ready. I can't stop to have any feelings, because that might cost me my life."

Rationally, that makes complete sense. When we're sympathetically activated, as long as we can use the flight or fight energy, fear doesn't really settle in. There probably is more focus, quicker decision making, maybe good decision making, the kind that keeps you alive and protects people. So that didn't disturb me at all.

Then he said, "Actually, there's one time when I do feel fear. It's when I'm activated for a call, and I'm sitting in my police car waiting for the parking lot gate to open. That's when I start to think about what could go wrong. That's when I think about how I might not make it through the situation."

blocks.h: Fear is mobilization that can't move

blocks.p: Why would sitting in his car, waiting for a slow gate, trigger fear in someone who otherwise says he doesn't feel fear on the job? He's perfectly safe in that moment, right?

It's because he's immobilized while in flight or fight. There's adrenaline in his system. The defensive energy is activated, coursing through his veins and his muscles. Biologically, he's ready to run or fight. He's primed for duty, ready to roll. But he can't advance to where he needs to go. He's stuck behind a slow-moving gate.
He only felt fear once he was immobilized while he had mobilization in his system, once he couldn't advance toward his directive.

On top of that, whatever polyvagal state we're in, our story follows our state. The thoughts in our brain follow the state we are in. In a safety state, your thoughts tend to be more positive, connective, empathetic, and hopeful. In a fight state, they're more about blame and anger, and maybe avoiding responsibility or putting it onto somebody else.

So for this officer, immobilized while in flight or fight, the thoughts in his mind take on a fearful, freeze kind of flavor. He's thinking about how he's not going to make it through. He's thinking about how he may not get home to his family, how he won't be able to help, how the worst thing is going to happen. All that flight or fight energy he's unable to use flavors his thoughts, and his thoughts become anxious, panicky, fearful.

blocks.h: What this has to do with your trauma work

blocks.p: Say you're doing the trauma work, whatever that looks like for you. You may have some fear in your system, and that fear gets there from having flight or fight energy while being immobilized.

People tell me this comes up in some yoga poses: they have mobility in their system, but they're immobilized. In a meditation, or in therapy while you're talking about whatever it is, flight or fight energy may come up, and there may be immobility too. Maybe that's because it feels like it's not okay to move in therapy. Maybe you're holding a certain pose in yoga. Maybe fear comes up in your own meditation practice and you're just frozen there in the moment. Mobility plus immobility: that's fear.
So when you set out to do your unstucking work, here are three things to help reduce the intensity of that fear. The first is longer term. The other two are short-term, immediate things you can do.

blocks.h: 1. Develop the strength of your safety state

blocks.p: You've heard me say this a lot. Your vagal brake must be strengthened before delving into your stuck defensive state. It is absolutely imperative. From what I can tell, therapists in general completely overlook this, and they expect, or even pressure, people to talk about their trauma narrative, the stuff they've been through, which ends up being re-traumatizing.
When you go into the stuck defensive state, there's a really good chance that freeze, or fear, will come along with whatever is inside of you. That's why the vagal brake has to be developed first.

Over the longer term, as you develop the strength of your vagal brake, the immobility of freeze, the immobility of fear, will thaw and let you feel and act on your mobility, your flight or fight energy. Or at least feel it, and allow some shifts to happen within you.

Safety anchors are the things that ground you in your safety state. To develop your vagal brake, you need to know what helps you feel safe. The more you practice with them, the more your vagal brake develops.
Look at them in two ways. Dr. Porges talks about this in his second book, I believe: passive safety anchors and active safety anchors.

Passive ones are in your environment. They bring you a cue of safety without you having to do anything or consciously notice them, although I think mindfully noticing them brings them to an active level and is more helpful. In my office I have some of my favorite stuff around me: some Lego builds, Venom and a Lego bonsai tree, a 49ers helmet from my childhood, Optimus Prime, all these nerdy things, plus my Polyvagal books, a couple of design books, some fake plants, some markers, a dim light. When I just see them, it's a cue of safety for me. There are things in there that have meaning for me, that are safe.

Active ones are things you do: some fidgeting, smelling something you find grounding, like an orange or a lemon or a lime, tasting something grounding, looking at something grounding. You'll have to differentiate what's passive and what's active for you.
Use both before you look more directly at your stuck defensive state.

blocks.why: This article talks about anchoring in safety. This practice does just that, tuned to you.

blocks.p: Third, give yourself some top-down safety anchors beforehand. Again, this is all before: before you start delving into your dysregulation, before you start that meditation or that therapeutic practice, whatever it is.
Top-down means things you send from your brain to your body: a thought, a memory, your imagination. It could be a thought like:

ul: "I deserve to live a life with more safety."
"I can handle this. I've prepared for this. I believe in myself, and I can handle whatever is inside of me."

blocks.p: You have to be honest with yourself about that, by the way. If you can't say it honestly, that's okay. Come back to it when you're ready. Or you could say something like, "Maybe this is going to be challenging. I want to know what's in there. I'm curious what the heck is happening inside of me. I believe in myself, or I'm at least curious. And if I need to stop, I know how to stop, and I'm allowed to pause this and come back to it when I'm ready."

I recommend putting all three together: the top-down thoughts, plus an environment of passive safety, plus something active that grounds you in safety. If you're not doing these things already, bring them to whatever you're doing, especially the passive and active safety anchoring. They're really, really helpful.
